index.para: This document specifies requirements for implementations of the Gear™ programming language version 1.0. It describes the representation of Gear programs, the syntax and constraints of the Gear language, and the restrictions and limits imposed by a conforming implementation of Gear. The specification does not describe the mechanism by which Gear is transformed into an executable program, the mechanism by which a Gear program is invoked, or the mechanism by which a host embedds Gear.
The latest canonical version of the specification can be obtained from: https://gear-lang.org/.
Defect reports for the specification should be filed on GitHub: https://github.com/gear-lang/spec/issues.

For dated references, only the edition cited applies. For undated references, the latest edition of the referenced document (including any amendments) applies.

ul.li: The Unicode Consortium. Unicode Standard Annex, UAX #15, Unicode Normalization Forms[online]. Edited by Ken Whistler. Revision 54; issued for Unicode 15.1.0. 2023-08-12. Available at https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr15/tr15-54.html

index.para: Conformance is of interest to the following audiences:

ul.li: Those designing, implementing, or maintaining Gear implementations.
Governmental or commercial entities wishing to procure Gear implementations.
Testing organizations wishing to provide a Gear conformance test suite.
Programmers wishing to port code from one Gear implementation to another.
Educators wishing to teach Gear.
Authors wanting to write about Gear.

index.para: As such, conformance is most important, and the bulk of this specification is aimed at specifying the characteristics that make Gear implementations and Gear programs conforming ones.

The text in this specification that specifies requirements is considered normative. All other text in this specification is informative; that is, for information purposes only. Unless stated otherwise, all text is normative. Normative text is further broken into required and conditional categories. Conditionally normative text specifies a feature and its requirements where the feature is optional. However, if that feature is provided, its syntax and semantics shall be exactly as specified.

A strictly conforming program shall use only those features of the language specified in this specification as being required. (This means that a strictly conforming program cannot use any conditionally normative feature). It shall not produce output dependent on any unspecified, undefined, or implementation-defined behavior. “Must” describes essential behavior that needs to be uniformly applied across all implementations. “Should” describes a strong recommendation, but is not required.
A conforming implementation of Gear shall accept any strictly conforming program.

A conforming implementation of Gear shall provide and support all the types, values, functions, and program syntax and semantics described in the normative (but not the conditionally normative) parts in this specification.

A conforming implementation of Gear is permitted to provide additional types, values, and functions beyond those described in this specification, provided they do not alter the behavior of any strictly conforming program.
A conforming implementation of Gear shall support the standard library documented in . This library is included by reference in this specification.
A conforming program is one that is acceptable to a conforming implementation.

Lexical and syntactic grammars for Gear are interspersed throughout this specification. The lexical grammar defines how characters can be combined to form tokens, the minimal lexical elements of the language. The syntactic grammar defines how tokens can be combined to make valid Gear programs.

Grammar productions include both non-terminal and terminal symbols. In grammar productions, non-terminal symbols are shown in italic type and terminal symbols are shown in fixed-width font. Each non-terminal is defined by a set of productions. The first line of a set of productions is the name of the non-terminal, followed by a colon. Each successive indented line contains the right-hand side for a production that has the non-terminal symbol as the left-hand side. For example:

Examples are provided to illustrate possible forms of the constructions described. References are used to refer to related clauses. Notes are provided to give advice or guidance to implementers or programmers. Annexes provide additional information and summarize the information contained in this Specification.

informative.para: Gear is a simple and small, type-safe, procedural programming language. Its syntax will be immediately familair to anyone with a background with C family programming language. Its small size is designed to mirror that of other small languages, like Lua and Go.

The rest of this chapter describes the essential features of the language. While later chapters describe rules and exceptions using formal language, this chapter strives for clarity and brevity at the expense of completeness. The intent is to provide the reader with an introduction to the language that will facilitate the writing of early programs and the reading of later chapters.

index.para: A Gear program consists of one or more compilation units. A compilation unit is an ordered sequence of Unicode characters. Compilation units typically have a one-to-one correspondence with source files in a file system, but this correspondence is not required.

A Gear compiler is a program that translates a Gear program into an executable form. When a Gear program is compiled, all of the compilation units are processed together. Compilation units can depend on each other, possibly in a circular fashion.
For compatibility with other tools, a Gear compiler may ignore the Byte Order Mark character (U+FEFF) if it is the first Unicode character in the source text.

For compatibility with source code editing tools that add end-of-file markers, and to enable a source file to be viewed as a sequence of properly terminated lines, if the last character of the source file is a Control-Z character (U+001A), the character is deleted.

The handling of the Unicode NUL character (U+0000) is implementation-defined. It is strongly recommended that developers avoid using this character in their source code, for the sake of portability and readability. When the character is required within a character or string literal, the escape sequences 0 or u0000 may be used.
It is beyond the scope of this standard to define how a file using a character representation other than Unicode might be transformed into a sequence of Unicode character.
White space is defined as any Unicode character with the property Pattern_White_Space.
Two forms of comments are supported: delimited comments and single-line comments.

delimited comment
A delimited comment begins with the characters * and ends with the characters */. They can occupy a portion of a line, a single line, or multiple lines. Delimited comments can nest.

single-line comment
A single-line comment begins with the // characters and extends to the end of the line. The character sequences * and */ has no special meaning within a single-line comment, and the character sequences // has no special meaning within a delimited comment.
Comments are not processed within string literals.

A lexical token is a string with an assigned meaning. In Gear there are several kinds of tokens: identifiers, keywords, literals, operators, and terminators. White space and comments are not tokens, though they act as separators for tokens.

Token matching is greedy which means the longest token that can be matched is matched. That means given the token stream += the operator is matched as-is in its entirety; it is not matched as two individual + and = tokens.

An identifier is an arbitrarily long sequence of letters, ideographs, and digits. Identifiers are case sensitive, that is, uppercase and lowercase letters are considered distinct. Identifiers are considered equivalent if they are canonically equivalent as described by UAX #15.
The character properties XID_Start and XID_Continue are Derived Core Properties as described by UAX #44.

alt.nobreak: any Unicode character with property XID_Start
any Unicode character with property XID_Continue

index.para: A keyword is an identifier-like sequence of characters that is reserved and cannot be used as an identifier.

section.title: Operators and punctuators
section.para: There are several kinds of operators and punctuators. Operators are used in expressions to describe operations involving one or more operands. Punctuators are for grouping and separating. Each operator and punctuator is converted to a single token.

section.title: Literals
section.para: A literal is a source code representation of a value.

index.para: In an integer-literal, the sequence of binary-digit, octal-digit, digit, or hexadecimal-digit, is interpreted as a base N integer as shown in table ; the lexically first digit of the sequence of digits is the most significant.
The hexadecimal-digit a through f and A through F have decimal values ten through fifteen.
index.example: The number twelve can be written 12, 0C14, 0XC, or 0b1100. The integer-literal 1048576, 0x100000, and 0c004000000 all have the same value.
index.para: The type of an integer-literal is Int.

The significand of a real-literal is the decimal-literal and fractional-part. In the significand, the sequence of digit and period are interpreted as base 10 real number s. If an exponent-part is present, the exponent e of the real-literal is the result of interpreting the sequence of an optional sign and the digit as a base 10 integer. Otherwise, the exponent e is 0. The scaled value of the literal is s times 10^e for a real-literal.
index.example: The real-literal 124.7 and 1.247e2 have the same value, as do 0.005600 and 5.600E-3.
index.para: If the scaled value is not in the range of representable values for its type, the program is ill-formed. Otherwise, the value of a real-literal is the scaled value if representable, else the larger or smaller representable value nearest the scaled value, chosen in an choice of larger or smaller value of real-literal manner.
The type of an real-literal is Real.

A character literal consists of exactly one Unicode scalar values enclosed in single quotation marks, as in 'a', and can include simple escape sequences (such as t for tab), hexadecimal, and Unicode escape sequences.

A Unicode scalar value is any code point in the Unicode code space except for surrogate characters. The Unicode code space is the inclusive integer range 016 to 10FFFF16. Unicode surrogate characters are those code points in the inclusive integer range D80016 to DBFF16 and DC0016 to DFFF16.
A Unicode escape sequence begins, excluding Unicode character escape sequences, begins with a backslash and is followed by one of. The substitute characters are listed in .

A Unicode character escape sequence begins with a u or U and is followed by four (4) or eight (8) hexidecimal digits, respectively. The sequence is replaced by the Unicode code point identified by the hexidecimal digits. It is erroneous if the code point is not a Unicode scalar value.

section.title: String literals
section.para: A string literal consists of zero or more Unicode scalar values enclosed in double quotation marks, as in "hello", and can include simple escape sequences (such as t for tab), hexadecimal, and Unicode escape sequences.
A string literal may contain an interpolation-expression which is an expression evaluated at runtime and inserted into the string. This process is documented .

index.para: The type of an boolean-literal is Bool.
The type of an nil-literal represents the absence of a value.
Terminators delimit productions. Line terminators are commonly added to improve readability. Semicolon terminators terminates are useful for termining multiple statements on the same line.

Line terminators divide the characters of a Gear source file into lines. The productions defined by this specification do not neccessarily include explicit line terminators, however, one or more shall be implictly assumed: at the beginning and end of every compilation unit; after every keyword, operator or punctuator token.

For compatibility with CR+LF line endings, if a carriage return character (U+000D) is immediately succeeded by a line feed character (U+000A), then they shall be processed as if they were a single new line character.

section.title: Semicolon terminators
section.para: The formal syntax uses the semicolon character (U+0042) as a terminator in a number of productions. Gear programs may substitute the semicolon for a line terminator.

section.title: Compiler Control Statements
section.para: A compilation unit may optionally include zero or more compiler control statements. A compiler control statement permits the compilation unit to change aspects of the compiler’s behavior. Gear has three compiler control statements: conditional compilation block, warning, and error control statements.

Compiler control statements are processed with the same precedence as strings and comments. Consequently, if a compiler control statement appears within a string, it is considered part of the string literal. Conversely, if such a statement is found within a comment, it is ignored and does not influence the compilation process.

Compiler control statements must appear at the beginning of a line and must start with a number sign (U+0023). The number sign is followed by an identifier (together the control keyword as listed in ) that designates the type of control statement.
This specification describes the precise semantics of compiler control statements in .

chapter.title: Basic concepts
chapter.para: Program execution begins when the execution environment calls a function, which is referred to as the program's entry point .

During program execution instructions or statements are sequentially executed in the order they are written in the source code. This means that the first statement is executed first, followed by the second, and so on, until the end of the sequence is reached. At any given point, only one instruction or statement can be executed. There is no overlap or simultaneous execution of multiple instructions.

Sequential execution can be altered using control flow constructs such as conditionals (if, switch), loops (for, while), and function calls, which can change the order in which statements are executed.

Program termination occurs after the last instruction or statement of the entry point has executed or the code panics without handling the panic. When program termination occurs control is returned to the execution environment.

section.title: Run-time panics
section.para: Execution errors such as attempting to divide by zero trigger a run-time panic equivalent to a call of the built-in function panic with a value of the implementation-defined interface type std.Error. The exact error values that represent distinct run-time error conditions are unspecified.

chapter.title: Types
chapter.para: A type determines a set of values together with operations and methods specific to those values. The types of the Gear language are divided into two main categories: reference types and value types. A reference type may be a generic type, which take one or more type parameters.

Value types differ from reference types in that variables of the value types directly contain their data, whereas variables of the reference types store references to their data. With reference types, it is possible for two variables to reference the same object, and thus possible for operations on one variable to affect the object referenced by the other variable. With value types, the variables each have their own copy of the data, and it is not possible for operations on one to affect the other. Value types may also have operators associated with them whereas reference types may not.

A type may be denoted by a type name, if it has one, which must be followed by type arguments if the type is generic. A type may also be specified using a type literal, which composes a type from existing types.
A type error occurs when a program construct cannot be assigned a type.

section.title: Named types
section.para: Named types are types declared with an identifier. The name of a type includes the modules it is declared in.
section.example: The declaration class Person { name: String } would define a record type named Person, but the type in the variable declaration var person: { name: String } is not named.
section.para: Value types are always named.

section.title: Intrinsic types
section.para: Intrinsic types are fundamental types directly supported by Gear and any underlying implementation. These types are always accessible and have operations that are also predefined.

section.title: Boolean types
section.para: A boolean type represents the set of Boolean truth values denoted by the keywords true and false. The boolean type is Bool.
Boolean types are value types.

section.title: Integer types
section.para: An integer type represents a continuous range of whole numbers without any fractional part. The minimum storage requirements for the integer type are 2^{32} bits. The representable range of the integer type, and its underlying format, are implementation-defined.

The integer type is named Int. Integers appear literally represented in source code according to the integer-literal grammar rule. Implementations must report an error or warning for integer literals outside the representable range. Implementations reporting a warning should clamp the integer to its minima or maxima.
Integer types are value types.

section.title: Real types
section.para: A real type represents a finite approximation of whole and fractional numbers. The representable range and fractional precision of a real type, and its underlying format, are implementation-defined.

The real type is named Real. Reals may be literally represented in source code according to the real-literal grammar rule. Implementations must report an error or warning for real literals outside the representable range. Implementations reporting a warning should clamp the real to its minima or maxima.
Real types are value types.

section.title: Character types
section.para: A character type represents the set of Unicode scalar values. The character type is Char.

Characters appear literally represented in source code according to the real-literal grammar rule. Implementations must report an error if a character literal describes a code point that is not a Unicode scalar value.
Character types are value types.

section.title: String types
section.para: A string type represents an immutable collection of zero or more characters. The underlying representation is implementation-defined.
The string type is String. Strings appear literally represented in source code according to the string-literal grammar rule.
String types are value types.

section.title: Function types
section.para: A function type denotes the set of all functions with the same parameter and result types.
It is erroneous for the last parameter in function-parameters to omit a type. The function type (a,b:Int) is valid, but (a:Int,b) is erroneous.

section.title: Object types
section.para: An object is a sequence of named elements, called fields, each of which has a name and a type. An object can have functions associated with it called methods.

section.title: Optional types
section.para: An optional type is a type constructor that encapsulates the possibility of a value being present or absent. It can contain a value of type T or represent the absence of a value by the special value nil.
Optional types are denoted by appending a question mark (?) to an existing type. This syntax indicates that the type can either be a value of the specified type or represent the absence of a value.
section.example: The type Int? represents a type that is either an integer or nil. The type Bool?? represents an optional type that might contain another optional type which might contain a boolean.

section.title: Parameterized Types
section.para: Parameterized types, or generic types, take type parameters and create new types based on those parameters. Type constructors allow for parametric polymorphism, where the new type is generic and can be instantiated with different type arguments.
Type constructors can take type parameters and create new types based on those parameters.

Type parameters must be one of the following: named interface type, inline record type, inline function type, intersection type, or an alias type to any of the aformentioned types. When instantiating a generic type the type arguments can be any type except an optional type.

section.title: Type compatibility
section.para: Type compatibility refers to the rules or conditions under which a type T can be substituted for another type S without resulting in a compile-time error. There are two aspects to type compatibility: subtyping and type equivalence. Subtyping refers to a relationship where one type (the subtype) is considered to be a specialization of another type (the supertype). Type equivalence refers to whether two types are considered the same for the purposes of type checking.

If type S is a subtype of type T (written as S<:T), then values of type T may be replaced with values of type S. If type S is type equivalent to type T (written as S≡T), then values of type T may be replaced with values of type S.

Type S may be type equivalent to type T by structural equivalence or nominal equivalence. When types are compared for structural equivalence it means equivalence is determined by the type's actual structure or definition and not by other characteristics such as its name. When types are compared for nominal equivalence it means equivalence is determined by the name of the types.
Unless otherwise noted in this specification a type S and a type T are never type compatible.

section.title: Value types
section.para: A value type T can be substituted for a value type S if all of the conditions apply:

ul.li: S and T are named types
S and T name the same type

section.title: Function types
section.para: A function type may be defined with parameter types \{p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_n\} and return type R. Let P=\{p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_n\}. Given a function type F denote its parameter types with F_P and its return type with F_R.
A function type T can be substituted for another function type S if all of the conditions apply:

ul.li: S and T have the same arity
TP <: SP
SR <: TR

section.title: Object types
section.para: When an object type is a value type it must conform to the type compatibility rules for value types. The remainder of this seciton defines type compatibility for when an object type is a reference type.
An object type may be defined with members \{m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_n\}. Let M=\{m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_n\}. Given a object type R denote its members types with R_M.
Formally, an object type T can be substituted for another object type S if all of the conditions apply:

ul.li: SM ⊆ TM
SM ≡ TM

section.title: Boxing and unboxing
section.para: Boxing refers to copying a value of a value type into a new value that is a reference type.

section.title: Boxing conventions
section.para: A boxing conversion permits a value type to be implicitly converted to a reference type. The following boxing conversions exist: From any value type to a variance-convertible reference type: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/conversions#1029-boxing-conversions

section.title: Unboxing conventions
section.para: An unboxing conversion permits a reference type to be implicitly converted to a value type. The following unboxing conversions exist: From any generic value type `V₀` to a value type `V`. An unboxing conversion permits a reference type to be explicitly converted to a value type. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/conversions#1037-unboxing-conversions

chapter.title: Identifiers and scope
chapter.para: Identifiers are names used to identify variables, functions, types, and other named entities within the language. An identifier serves as a symbolic name that binds to a specific entity in the language, allowing programmers to reference and manipulate that entity throughout the code. An identifier is entered in source code using the identifier lexical token.

Name binding refers to the association of an identifier with an entity, such as data or code. Name binding establishes a relationship where the identifier acts as a reference to the underlying entity.

“Scope” refers to the set of all name bindings that are valid within a part of a program or at a given point in a program. Scope is determined by the lexical structure of the code. Lexical scoping is the mechanism used to determine the visibility and lifetime of identifiers based on the program's textual structure. Under lexical scoping, the scope of an identifier is determined by its position in the source code and the nesting of code blocks, rather than the execution flow.

A declaration creates a name binding to a constant, type, type parameter, variable, function, or module. Every identifier in a program must be declared. No identifier may be declared twice in the same scope.

section.title: Block scope
section.para: A block is a possibly empty sequence of declarations and statements within matching brace brackets. Each block defines a new scope.

When a block is declared in another block the former is referred to as the inner block and the latter is the outer block. An identifier declared in an outer block is visible to all inner (nested) blocks if its declaration precedes the inner block declaration in the textual order of the code.

Declarations outside any block occur at module scope.

chapter.title: Expressions
chapter.para: An expression specifies the computation of a value by applying operators and functions to operands.

section.title: Assignment
section.para: An assignment replaces the current value stored in a identifier with a new value specified by an expression. An assignment statement may assign a single value to a single variable, or multiple values to a matching number of variables.

section.title: Operators
section.para: Expressions are constructed from operands and operators. The operators of an expression indicate which operations to apply to the operands. Examples of operators include +, -, *, and /. Examples of operands include literals, fields, local variables, and expressions.
There are three kinds of operators:

ul.li: Unary operators. The unary operators take one operand and use either prefix notation (such as -x) or postfix notation (such as x++).
Binary operators. The binary operators take two operands and all use infix notation (such as x + y)
Ternary operator. Only one ternary operator, ?:, exists; it takes three operands and uses infix notation (c ? x : y).

section.para: The order of evaluation of operators in an expression is determined by the precedence and associativity of the operators.
The order in which operands in an expression are evaluated, is left to right.

Certain operators can be overloaded. Operator overloading permits user-defined operator implementations to be specified for operations where one or both of the operands are of a user-defined class or struct type.

section.title: Operator precedence and associativity
section.para: When an expression contains multiple operators, the precedence of the operators controls the order in which the individual operators are evaluated. The precedence of an operator is established by the definition of its associated grammar production.
The following table summarizes all operators in order of precedence from highest to lowest:

When an operand occurs between two operators with the same precedence, the associativity of the operators controls the order in which the operations are performed. All operators are left-associative, meaning that operations are performed from left to right.
Precedence and associativity can be controlled using parentheses.
section.example: The expression x + y * z first multiplies y by z and then adds the result to x, but (x + y) * z first adds x and y and then multiplies the result by z.

section.title: Primary expressions
section.para: Primary expressions include every form of expression.

Primary expressions are divided between expressions and record-creation-expressions. Treating record-creation-expression in this way, rather than listing it along with the other expression forms, enables the grammar to disallow potentially confusing code such as

which could be interpreted as an “if” statement with a conditional x and an empty block or as an incomplete “if” statement where the condition expression constructs a record named x with default field initialization.

section.title: Objects
section.para: Anonymous objects types can be declared and instantiated using the class keyword. Methods implictly receive the object instance through the contextual keyword: Low Line (U+005F) character.

section.title: Try
section.para: Here try is a unary operator.

section.title: Try-else
section.para: Here a try-else is a binary operation accepting two operands: the first expression which might error and the second expression which is returned if the function does here.

section.title: Catch
section.para: Here block will be entered if expression errors. If block does not return control and expression errors, then nil is returned.

index.para: In Gear, there are three kinds of statements: simple statements, compiler control statements, and control flow statements. Simple statements are the most common and consist of either an expression or a declaration. Compiler control statements allow the program to change aspects of the compiler’s behavior and include a conditional compilation block and a line control statement.

Control flow statements are used to control the flow of execution in a program. There are several types of control flow statements in Swift, including loop statements, branch statements, and control transfer statements. Loop statements allow a block of code to be executed repeatedly, branch statements allow a certain block of code to be executed only when certain conditions are met, and control transfer statements provide a way to alter the order in which code is executed. In addition, Gear provides a defer statement for running cleanup actions just before the current scope exits.
A semicolon (;) can optionally appear after any statement and is used to separate multiple statements if they appear on the same line.

section.title: Selection statements
section.para: Selection statements allow the program to execute certain blocks of code depending on the value of one or more conditions. The values of the conditions specified in a selection statement control how the program branches and, therefore, what block of code is executed. Gear has two selection statements: an if statement and a switch statement.

section.title: If statement
section.para: “If” statements specify the conditional execution of two blocks according to the value of a boolean expression. If the expression evaluates to bold{true}, the “if” block is executed, otherwise, if present, the “else” block is executed.

If the “if” statement is of the form if var, then conditional execution is determined by whether the variables are non-null. A variable declared with an explicit type annotation is matched according to the pattern matching rules.
A if statement is executed as follows:

ul.li: The expression is evaluated.
If expression yields true, control is transferred to block.
If expression yields false, control is transferred to the optional else which may be another “if” statement or the “else” block.

section.title: Switch statement
section.para: “Switch” statements provide multi-way execution. An expression or type is compared to the "cases" inside the "switch" to determine which branch to execute. If no case matches and there is a "default" case, its statements are executed. There can be at most one default case and it may appear anywhere in the "switch" statement.
A switch statement is executed as follows:

ul.li: The switch expression is evaluated.
If the switch expression yields a value that matches a case expression, control is transferred to its block.

If the switch expression yields a value that does not match any case expression, control is transferred to the optional default. If there is no optional default, control is transferred to the end point of the switch statement.

section.title: Iteration statement
section.para: Iteration statements repeatedly execute a block.

section.title: While statement
section.para: The “while” statement conditionally executes a block zero or more times.
A while statement is executed as follows:

ul.li: The expression is evaluated.

If expression yields true, control is transferred to the block. When and if control reaches the end point of the block (possibly from execution of a continue statement), control is transferred to the beginning of the while statement.
If expression yields false, control is transferred to the end point of the while statement.

section.para: Within the block of a while statement, a break statement may be used to transfer control to the end point of the while statement (thus ending iteration of the block), and a continue statement may be used to transfer control to the end point of the block statement (thus performing another iteration of the while statement).

section.title: Do statement
section.para: The “do” statement conditionally executes a block zero or more times.
A do statement is executed as follows:

ul.li: Control is transferred to the block.

When and if control reaches the end point of the block (possibly from execution of a continue statement), the expressionis evaluated. If the expression yields true, control is transferred to the beginning of the do statement. Otherwise, control is transferred to the end point of the do statement.

Within the block of a do statement, a break statement may be used to transfer control to the end point of the do statement (thus ending iteration of the block), and a continue statement may be used to transfer control to the end point of the block (thus performing another iteration of the do statement).

section.title: For statement
section.para: The “for” statement executes a block of code for any object that conforms to the Sequence protocol.
A for statement is executed as follows:

ul.li: The expression is evaluated.

If expression yields an iterator object conforming to the Sequence protocol, control is transferred to the next() method of the iterator object. If the value returned by next() isn’t nil, it’s assigned to the identifier pattern and control is transferred to the block. If the value returned by next() is nil, control is transferred to the end point of the for statement.

When and if control reaches the end point of the block (possibly from execution of a continue statement), the next() method of the iterator object is evaluated again (thus performing another iteration of the for statement).

section.title: Jump statements
section.para: Jump statements unconditionally transfer control.
The location to which a jump statement transfers control is called the target of the jump statement

When a jump statement occurs within a block, and the target of that jump statement is outside that block, the jump statement is said to exit the block. While a jump statement may transfer control out of a block, it can never transfer control into a block

section.title: Break statement
section.para: The “break” statement exits the nearest enclosing switch , while, do, or for statement.

The target of a break statement is the end point of the nearest enclosing switch, while, do, or for statement. If a break statement is not enclosed by a switch, while, do, or for statement, a compile-time error occurs.
When multiple switch, while, do, or for statements are nested within each other, a breakstatement applies only to the innermost statement.
A break statement is executed as follows:

ul.li: Control is transferred to the target of the break statement.

section.para: Because a break statement unconditionally transfers control elsewhere, the end point of a break statement is never reachable

section.title: Continue statement
section.para: The “continue” statement starts a new iteration of the nearest enclosing switch, while, do, or for statement.

The target of a continue statement is the end point of the block statement of the nearest enclosing while, do, or for statement. If a continue statement is not enclosed by a while, do, or for statement, a compile-time error occurs.
When multiple while, do, or for statements are nested within each other, a continuestatement applies only to the innermost statement.
A continue statement is executed as follows:

ul.li: Control is transferred to the target of the continue statement.

section.para: Because a continue statement unconditionally transfers control elsewhere, the end point of a continue statement is never reachable.

section.title: Return statement
section.para: The “return” statement returns control to the caller of the function member in which the return statement appears.
A return statement with no expression can be used only in a function that does not compute a value; that is, a function with the return type void.
A return statement with an expression can only be used in a function that computes a value; that is, a function with a non-void return type.
A return statement is executed as follows:

ul.li: If the return statement specifies an expression, the expression is evaluated and the resulting value is converted to the return type of the containing function member by an implicit conversion. The result of the conversion becomes the value returned to the caller.
Control is returned to the caller of the containing function member.

section.para: Because a return statement unconditionally transfers control elsewhere, the end point of a return statement is never reachable.

section.title: Defer statements
section.para: A “defer” statement evaluates an expression or block whose execution is deferred to the moment the enclosing block exits, either because the enclosing block executed a return statement, a break statement, a continue statement, or control reached the end of its block, or because the corresponding thread panicked.
A defer statement is executed as follows:

ul.li: The defer statement is executed the moment the enclosing block exits.
If there is more than one defer statement in the enclosing block, they are evaluated in the reverse order of their position in the source code.
If control never reaches the defer statement, then the expression or block is not executed.

section.para: If a block contains a return statement, then a compile-time error occurs.

section.title: Use statements
section.para: A “use” statement facilitate the use of modules, types, and variables defined in other modules.

index.para: A compiler control statement allow the program to change aspects of the compiler’s behavior. Gear has three compiler control statements: a conditional compilation block, a warning and error control statements.
Every conditional compilation block begins with the #if compilation directive and ends with the #endif compilation directive. A simple conditional compilation block has the following form:

Unlike the condition of an if statement, the compilation condition is evaluated at compile time. As a result, the statements are compiled and executed only if the compilation condition evaluates to true at compile time. Tokens enclosed by a conditional compilation block are either included or excluded from compilation depending upon whehter the condition is true or false, respectivly. Tokens excluded from compilation are eneither parsed nor semanticly analyzied, and no diagnostic message are generated for them.

chapter.title: Declarations
chapter.para: A declaration binds an identifier to a constant, type, type parameter, variable, function, or module. Every identifier in a program must be declared. No identifier may be declared twice in the same block.

section.title: Variable declaration
section.para: A variable declaration declares a variable which is a symbolic name associated with a value or a reference that can be used to store and manipulate data within a program. The value or reference held by the variable may be subject to change during the execution of the program, and the variable's name serves as an identifier to access and interact with the associated data. The scope of a variable is determined by its declaration context.

If the variable declaration includes an else block, then conditional execution of the block is determined by whether the variable(s) are non-null. All variables declared with an explicit type annotation are matched according to the pattern matching rules. The block must use termination statement(s) (e.g. return, break, continue) to terminate the enclosing block.
Examples of variable declarations include:
section.code: var n: Int? var s = "Hello" var b: Bool = true var x = 1, y: Int = 2, z: Int?

section.title: Module declaration
section.para: Gear programs are organized using modules. Modules are used both as an "`internal`" organization system for a program, and as an "`external`" organization system -- a way of presenting program elements that are exposed to other programs. Use directives are provided to facilitate the use of modules.
Every module and type declaration has a fully qualified name, which uniquely identifies the module or type declaration amongst all others within the program.

A module declaration consists of the keyword module followed by the module name. If the module has a body (see module-body), then only the enclosed declarations are added to the module. Otherwise, the module applies to all declarations in the compilation unit.
Only one module without a body can be declared in a compilation unit otherwise it is an error.

The fully qualified module name (see module-name) is added to the global scope unless there is a module without a body in which case all modules with a body are added to the scope of the module without a body.
Modules are open-ended, and two module declarations with the same fully qualified name contribute to the same declaration space.

section.title: Function declaration
section.para: A function type denotes the set of all functions with the same parameter and result types. Informally, they are a sequence of zero or more statements that accept input and produce an output.
Functions as discussed in this chapter are statements, however, they can also be expressions as discussed ref{here}.

Free functions may be associated with a record type. The record to associate a function with is named by ident-type of the func-prefix production rule. If the association has an identifier, then it is receieves the record when invoked and is accessible by the label identifier.

section.title: Class declaration
section.para: A class is a composite data structure that contains fields and methods together known as members. Members may be specified explicitly or implicitly (see embedded members).
Classes are declared with the class keyword, followed by a name, followed by a class-body. The class-body defines the fields and embedded members.

The record name defined by the ident in record-header is inserted into scope of the module in which is it was declared. It is also inserted into the scope of the record itself. This permits the record to be self-referenced as a field, see type of fields-decl.

section.title: Interface declaration
section.para: An interface is a named <<record-type,record type>>. They are declared with the interface keyword.
Interfaces can be instantiated so long as there is an inline implementation provided for each method at the call site. See <<object-instantiation,object instantiation>>.
Unlike a record type, an interface can mixin the contents of one or more interfaces.
The primary difference between an interface and a struct is the former can be mixed and the latter can embed fields.

section.title: Struct declaration
section.para: A struct is a named <<record-type,record type>> declared on a the stack instead of the heap. Structs cannot mixin interfaces and they do not allow embedding. They are _nominally typed_.

chapter.para: A class is a composite type.

section.title: Embedded members
section.para: Embedded members are part of the classes interface.

A selector f may denote a field or method f of a type T, or it may refer to a field or method f of a nested embedded field of T. The number of embedded fields traversed to reach f is called its depth in T. The depth of a field or method f declared in T is zero. The depth of a field or method f declared in an embedded field A in T is the depth of f in A plus one.
Promoted fields act like ordinary fields of a class except that they cannot be used as field names

section.title: Methods
section.para: Methods are functions semantically scoped to a class. Where left and right are self-referential fields.

annex.title: Implementation considerations
annex.para: The specification focuses on defining the expected behavior and observable outcomes of the Gear programming language. It specifies how Gear should operate from a functional and user-oriented perspective, but it does not prescribe the internal mechanisms or implementation details that achieve this behavior. While the specification defines the core behavior of the Gear language, real-world constraints and optimizations often necessitate additional considerations. This section offers practical guidance for implementers as well as strategies, algorithms, and optimizations to fulfill the described behavior. These considerations are intended to support implementers in adhering to the language’s principles while accommodating practical requirements.

section.title: Parsing source text
section.para: Gear source text may be processed using a canonical LR(1) parser. This parser can either be written by hand or automatically generated using parser generation tools. Because conforming implementations must support the Unicode character repertoire, any parser generation tool must itself be Unicode conformant. Parser generation tools that only support ASCII may not be used.

section.title: Numeric representation
section.para: The specification defines two numeric types: Int and Real. The specification designates their underlying representation as implementation-defined to provide the greatest degree of flexibility. There are several approaches available for digitally approximating real number values. Examples include the IEEE 754 floating-point standard, type III unums (posits), and fixed-point. Examples for representing integer values include signed magnitude representation, one’s complement, and two’s complement. The aforementioned formats are supported by modern hardware and therefore represent the most practical and efficient approach to representing numeric values.

To simulate a wider range of numeric values beyond what is traditionally supported by hardware requires a software solution. Implementations may spport arbitrary-precision arithmetic. This approach is limited only by the available memory rather than by fixed-size data types supported by the hardware. This approach provides the greatest degree of flexability, but at a performance cost.

section.title: String representation
section.para: The Unicode Standard defines several approaches to encoding text: UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32. UTF-32 encodes each character as a fixed-length 32-bit integer. This fixed length simplifies character indexing and manipulation but consumes more memory relative to UTF-8 and UTF-16. UTF-16 uses one or two 16-bit integers to encode each character. It is more space efficent than UTF-32, but characters cannot be indexed in constant time. UTF-8 uses one to four bytes to encode each charater. Is is more space efficent for Latin text relative to UTF-16, but decoding characters is more computation expensive and characters cannot be indexed in constant time.

String must provide operations for indexing characters therefore careful considerations must be made when implementation strings. The simpliest approach is to choose one of the aformentioned encodings. Alternatively, implementations may represent each character as 8-bits, 16-bits, or 32-bits depending on the characters involved. This approach saves memory for Latin characters and characters in the Basic Multilingual Plane.

The String type is a value type. This specification states that value types are copied, however, copying strings - especially longer strings - would introduce an unneccessary performance overhead and increase memory pressure. Because this specification defines strings to be immutable, implementations may internally treat them as references types. An implementation may also deduplicate strings in memory with string interning.

section.title: Conditional compilation blocks
section.para: Compiler control statements, comments, and strings must be processed together. Conceptually, this processing — along with the removal of conditionally excluded source text — occurs prior to any other analysis. This approach results in a two-pass tokenization process: the first pass handles compiler control statements, comments, and strings, generating new source text with the excluded text removed. The second pass performs lexical analysis on this cleaned source text.

To streamline the process and avoid generating new source text, tokens can be processed into a list during the first pass. Tokenization diagnostics can be appended directly to the relevant tokens. Unrecognized tokens may be represented as special, implementation-specific “invalid” tokens in the list.

After constructing the complete token list, it can be iterated to remove tokens excluded by conditional control statements evaluating to false. The final list, including all tokens and associated diagnostics, can be analyized.
